 4 weather alerts in effect Why Some Heber-Overgaard neighbors say tornado warning came too late 
 Some residents in the Heber-Overgaard area say a wireless emergency alert warning them about a tornado came too late. By Amy Cutler Published : Oct. 22, 2026 at 6:06 PM MST | Updated : 14 hours ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google HEBER-OVERGAARD, AZ (AZFamily) — Some residents in the Heber-Overgaard area say a wireless emergency alert warning them about a tornado came too late. It meant they didn’t have time to prepare before a suspected tornado touched down Wednesday evening. 
 National Weather Service meteorologists say, on average, its warnings are issued 8 to 15 minutes before a weather event.
 Courtney Shull was at her Overgaard home with her two kids Wednesday evening when an alert popped up on her cell phone at 7:04pm. The alert warned of a tornado warning and urged her to seek shelter immediately.
 “I did not feel prepared at all,” Shull said.
 “I couldn’t even click on the link to read any further details on it. So, I hurried up and grabbed my kids, my daughter was sleeping,” Shull said.
 Three minutes later, Shull received a call from Navajo County about the warning, telling her to find an interior room.
 “You’re rushing around trying to figure out what to do,” Shull said.
 She headed to the bathroom and huddled with her son, daughter and their 100-pound dog.
 “We just locked in there and again we had no service, so I had no way to check and see if it hit, is it passed, like are we safe to come out,” Shull said.
 National Weather Service response
 Mark O’Malley, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Phoenix, said the agency’s warning went out at 7:02pm, but it takes a couple of minutes for cell phone companies to issue those alerts.
 Asked about residents who said they didn’t get enough time, O’Malley said, “We put out the warnings in this case when the tornado was detected on radar.”
 “When the tornado forms immediately underneath the thunderstorm and the first indications are when the radar indicates it, and there can be as little as a few minutes warning,” O’Malley said.
 Timeline of the warning
 Shull’s text shows she received the message at 7:04pm. Determining the exact time the tornado touched down is tricky. The fire district says it was between 7:15pm and 7:25pm. The first 911 call came in at 7:18pm, meaning neighbors had at least 10 minutes notice.
 “Thankfully where we’re at, we’re about a mile, mile and a half away from where it touched down,” Shull said.
 Shull said they waited more than 30 minutes before she was finally able to call her mom and get the all clear.
 “I will be more prepared today. I’ve already got my bathroom all set up,” Shull said.
 The fire district said the first 911 call was about downed power lines. 911 calls reporting a man down came in 10 minutes later.
 Website used by first responders decommissioned
 A website first responders use for additional information on storms has been decommissioned. A National Weather Service meteorologist said the agency just learned about it too. The meteorologist said the issue is unrelated to the weather and involves a hack. First responders will still get alerts on their phones but won’t be able to access the maps and other features on the website. The National Weather Service is working on a fix.
